lesson.title: Writing a Conclusion That Actually Says Something
lesson.summary: A complete regression conclusion restates the decision about H0 in context, reports the direction and size of the relationship, and is honest about whether the study design supports a causal claim.
lesson.body:
A bare 'reject H0' or 'p < 0.0001' isn't a conclusion anyone outside a statistics class can use. A complete regression conclusion translates the math back into the original context: it states the decision about H0, reports the direction and, ideally, the size of the estimated relationship, and does all of this using the actual variables from the problem rather than generic symbols. This is the same structure expected of any hypothesis test conclusion, applied specifically to a slope.

A reliable template: because the p-value ([value]) is [less than / greater than] alpha ([value]), we [reject / fail to reject] H0. There is [strong / some / little] evidence of a [positive / negative] linear relationship between [x] and [y] in the population [described], with each additional [unit of x] associated with [b1] more or fewer [unit of y], on average.

Applying it to the running example: because the p-value (less than 0.0001) is far less than alpha (0.05), we reject H0: β1 = 0. There is strong evidence of a positive linear relationship between hours studied and quiz score, with each additional hour of studying associated with about 1.8 more points on the quiz, on average (95% confidence interval: 1.50 to 2.10 points).

One caution belongs in every such conclusion, and it connects directly back to the independence condition and to observational studies: this hours-studied dataset, like most study-time-and-score data, comes from an observational study. The students were not randomly assigned how much to study, so the honest conclusion describes an association, not a proven cause. It's entirely possible that more conscientious or better-prepared students both study more and score higher for reasons that have nothing directly to do with the extra hours themselves, a confounding explanation the data can't rule out. Only a genuine experiment, one that randomly assigns study time to different students, would license a causal claim like 'studying more causes higher scores.' This is a frequent trap: a tiny p-value is strong evidence that a relationship exists, but it says nothing at all about whether that relationship is causal, that distinction rides entirely on the study's design, not on the size of the t-statistic or p-value.

One more limit to flag honestly: 'strong evidence of a relationship' is a statement purely about whether the slope is zero. It says nothing about whether the relationship is large enough to actually matter in practice. Answering that second question is exactly the job of the next few chapters.
